triage.name: Crohn's Disease
triage.reason: Chronic inflammatory bowel disease with abdominal pain, diarrhea and weight loss; diagnosis reached by history, exam, labs, imaging and endoscopy.

demographics: More common in developed countries and urban areas
Higher incidence in people of Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry

risk_factors.text: Family history of inflammatory bowel disease

family_history: Inflammatory bowel disease in a first-degree relative

chief_complaints.text: My stomach has been cramping and hurting
I'm having loose, watery stools several times a day
I feel exhausted even when I rest

hpi.onset: Insidious over weeks to months; symptoms come and go
hpi.duration: Often present for months before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Recurrent crampy abdominal pain and diarrhea that wax and wane; weight loss and fatigue develop with ongoing inflammation
hpi.location: Most often right lower quadrant (terminal ileum), but can be periumbilical or diffuse
hpi.quality: Crampy and intermittent; may be steady aching during severe flares
hpi.timing: Cramping often after meals; diarrhea may occur multiple times daily and can wake the patient at night
pertinent_negatives: Vomiting that began before the pain
Pain that migrated from the umbilicus to the right lower quadrant over 12–24 hours
Sick contacts with similar acute diarrheal illness

positives.text: Tender red bumps on the shins
Painful skin ulcer with purple edge

atypical.how_it_differs: Often presents with growth failure, delayed puberty, and malabsorption, and may have more extensive disease with less prominent diarrhea. Abdominal pain may be vague.
May present with new colitis or perianal disease without typical long-standing diarrhea; symptoms can be milder and mistaken for ischemic colitis or diverticulitis.

general.mild: Well-appearing, may have mild abdominal discomfort but no acute distress
general.moderate: Appears uncomfortable, may be tired, lies still or guards abdomen
general.severe: Ill-appearing, cachectic, diaphoretic, in significant pain
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, pale, lethargic, may have signs of hypovolemia or sepsis

findings.maneuver: Palpate all four quadrants, starting away from the most painful area
findings.finding: Right lower quadrant tenderness or generalized abdominal tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the abdomen lightly and deeply
findings.finding: Voluntary guarding of the abdominal wall

findings.maneuver: Ask patient to cough or gently shake the bed; avoid deep palpation release if not necessary
findings.finding: Rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant

findings.maneuver: Deep palpation of the right lower quadrant
findings.finding: Tender, firm mass in the right lower quadrant (inflamed bowel or abscess)
Hyperactive bowel sounds, especially during diarrhea

findings.maneuver: Inspect the perianal area and perform digital rectal exam

findings.finding: Sentinel skin tag or large edematous skin tag
Aphthous ulcers on the buccal mucosa or tongue
Tender, red subcutaneous nodules on the shins

findings.maneuver: Inspect the skin, especially around stomas or legs
findings.finding: Painful ulcer with violaceous undermined edge

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the joints, especially knees, ankles, wrists
Palpate the right upper quadrant during inspiration
Percuss the liver span and palpate for the spleen
findings.finding: Liver and spleen are not enlarged

findings.maneuver: Examine the neck veins with the patient at 45 degrees

labs.caveat: Anemia may be from iron deficiency, chronic disease, or B12/folate deficiency.
Leukocytosis can accompany active inflammation; normal WBC does not exclude Crohn's.
Thrombocytosis is a nonspecific acute-phase response.
Correlates with disease activity; a normal CRP does not rule out Crohn's.
Less specific than CRP; may be elevated in many inflammatory states.
Low albumin reflects chronic inflammation and malnutrition.

findings.text: Skip lesions (patchy inflammation with normal mucosa between affected areas)
Aphthous ulcers and linear or serpiginous ulcers
Segmental bowel wall thickening with hyperenhancement

imaging.preferred_when: Young patients, pregnancy, repeated imaging (no radiation)

findings.text: Segmental bowel wall thickening with hyperenhancement

imaging.preferred_when: Older method for small bowel imaging when CT/MR not available
Suspected small bowel disease not seen on ileocolonoscopy or cross-sectional imaging

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected abscess, perforation, or acute complication

initial.why: Check for anemia, leukocytosis, and thrombocytosis
Marker of inflammation, useful with CRP
Rule out C. difficile infection, especially if recent antibiotics or hospitalization

confirmatory.why: Direct visualization and histology are required for diagnosis

supporting.why: Assesses small bowel involvement and complications
supporting.only_if: small bowel disease is suspected or colonoscopy incomplete
small bowel disease is suspected and radiation avoidance is important (young patient, pregnancy)

supporting.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
supporting.only_if: acute abdomen, abscess, or perforation is suspected
perianal fistula or abscess is suspected

supporting.why: Older method for small bowel imaging
supporting.only_if: cross-sectional imaging is unavailable or inconclusive

supporting.why: Visualizes small bowel mucosa not reached by endoscopy
supporting.only_if: suspected small bowel disease is not seen on other studies
upper GI symptoms or suspected proximal disease

decision_points: Pregnancy test before CT or MR enterography in any patient who could be pregnant
Cross-sectional imaging is indicated if there are signs of obstruction, abscess, or fistula
Colonoscopy with biopsy is required for diagnosis; do not diagnose Crohn's disease from imaging alone

criteria.name: Clinical-endoscopic-histologic diagnosis
criteria.summary: Diagnosis requires compatible clinical features, endoscopic findings, histopathology, and exclusion of other causes.
items: Chronic or recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms such as abdominal pain, diarrhea, and weight loss
Endoscopic findings of skip lesions, cobblestoning, or aphthous ulcers
Histopathology showing chronic inflammation, crypt distortion, or noncaseating granulomas
Imaging supportive of small bowel involvement
Exclusion of infectious colitis, ulcerative colitis, and other mimics

differential.name: Ulcerative colitis
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, abdominal pain, and weight loss; the other major inflammatory bowel disease

history: Bloody diarrhea is usually more prominent and continuous
exam: Tenderness often most prominent in the left lower quadrant
labs: ANCA may be positive, but not diagnostic
Fecal calprotectin is elevated in both conditions
imaging: Continuous inflammation starting in the rectum and extending proximally

differential.name: Clostridioides difficile colitis
differential.why_considered: Diarrhea, abdominal pain, fever, and elevated inflammatory markers can mimic an acute Crohn's flare
differential.trigger: Recent antibiotic or healthcare exposure with diarrhea and leukocytosis

history: Acute onset over days rather than weeks
Watery diarrhea may be profuse and sometimes bloody
exam: Toxic appearance may occur with severe disease
labs: Stool C. difficile toxin or PCR positive
imaging: Pancolitis with mucosal thickening on CT
No skip lesions or small bowel involvement

differential.name: Irritable bowel syndrome
differential.why_considered: Chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel habits without blood or weight loss

exam: Normal abdominal exam or mild tenderness without guarding
labs: No anemia or elevated CRP or ESR
imaging: Normal colonoscopy and small bowel imaging

differential.name: Celiac disease
differential.why_considered: Chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and fatigue

history: Diarrhea may be frothy or steatorrheal
Symptoms improve on a gluten-free diet
imaging: Small bowel folds may show atrophy on barium study or capsule endoscopy

differential.name: Acute appendicitis
differential.why_considered: Right lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis; terminal ileitis can mimic or cause appendicitis
differential.trigger: Acute right lower quadrant pain, especially with migratory pain and peritoneal signs

history: Pain starts periumbilical then migrates to right lower quadrant
imaging: Appendicolith and periappendiceal fat stranding on CT without terminal ileum thickening

differential.name: Intestinal tuberculosis
differential.why_considered: Chronic ileocecal inflammation with skip lesions, strictures, and fistulas
differential.trigger: Immigrant from TB-endemic area, active pulmonary TB, or ileocecal involvement

history: Travel or immigration from an endemic region
labs: Ascitic fluid AFB smear or culture may be positive
imaging: Ileocecal involvement with concentric narrowing and shorter stricture
Chest X-ray may show cavitary pulmonary tuberculosis

severity.mild: Fewer than 4 stools per day, no systemic symptoms, no significant abdominal tenderness, and normal inflammatory markers
severity.moderate: 4–6 loose stools per day, intermittent crampy pain, mild anemia, low-grade fever, and elevated CRP; responsive to outpatient treatment
severity.severe: More than 6 bloody stools per day, severe abdominal pain, fever above 100.4°F, anemia with hemoglobin below 10 g/dL, and low albumin; may require hospitalization
severity.critical: Fulminant colitis with toxic megacolon, perforation, sepsis, or massive hemorrhage; requires ICU care and urgent surgical evaluation

red_flags.finding: High fever with hypotension or tachycardia
Diffuse abdominal tenderness with rebound or rigidity
Colonic dilatation greater than 6 cm on imaging
red_flags.meaning: Toxic megacolon; urgent surgery may be needed

red_flags.finding: Obstipation with vomiting and abdominal distention
red_flags.meaning: Bowel obstruction from stricture or phlegmon

special_populations.differences: Often presents with growth failure, delayed puberty, and malabsorption; may have more extensive upper GI involvement and perianal disease. Exclusive enteral nutrition is often used for induction.
May present with new colitis or perianal disease without typical long-standing symptoms; higher risk of colorectal cancer and infections. Ischemic colitis and diverticulitis are important mimics.
Active disease can cause preterm birth and low birth weight; prefer MR enterography over CT. Flares are more likely if disease was active at conception; many drugs must be adjusted.
Increased risk of opportunistic infections during immunosuppressive therapy; screen for latent infections before starting biologics.

key_questions.question: When did your symptoms start, and how long have they been going on?
key_questions.looking_for: Insidious onset over weeks to months; chronic or recurrent course rather than acute onset

key_questions.question: Where is your abdominal pain located?
key_questions.looking_for: Right lower quadrant pain most common; may be periumbilical or diffuse

key_questions.question: How many loose stools are you having each day, and have they woken you up from sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Frequent loose stools, often nocturnal, consistent with inflammation

key_questions.question: Have you seen any blood or mucus in your stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Blood may be present but less prominent than in ulcerative colitis; mucus may occur

key_questions.question: Have you been losing weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Unintentional weight loss from malabsorption and inflammation

key_questions.question: Any nausea, vomiting, or loss of appetite?
key_questions.looking_for: Nausea and anorexia are common; vomiting suggests obstruction

key_questions.question: Do you have any joint pain, eye redness or pain, or tender bumps on your shins?
key_questions.looking_for: Extraintestinal manifestations (arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum) support Crohn's

key_questions.question: Any perianal pain, drainage, or skin tags?
key_questions.looking_for: Fistula, abscess, or fissure strongly suggests Crohn's

key_questions.question: Have you had recent antibiotics or been hospitalized?
key_questions.looking_for: Recent antibiotics or healthcare exposure raises concern for C. difficile; must be ruled out

key_questions.question: Do you take NSAIDs such as ibuprofen or naproxen?
key_questions.looking_for: NSAIDs can trigger or worsen Crohn's and may cause NSAID-induced enteropathy

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have inflammatory bowel disease?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history increases risk of Crohn's disease

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or did you smoke?
key_questions.looking_for: Cigarette smoking is a strong risk factor and worsens disease

key_questions.question: Have you traveled recently or been exposed to anyone with diarrhea?
key_questions.looking_for: Infectious colitis must be ruled out; travel or sick contacts suggest infection

key_questions.question: Are you able to keep down fluids? Have you been vomiting or stopped passing gas or stool?
key_questions.looking_for: Vomiting, obstipation, or severe distention suggests bowel obstruction

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy affects imaging choice and management

reasoning_points: Chronic or recurrent gastrointestinal symptoms (abdominal pain, diarrhea, weight loss) lasting weeks to months
Right lower quadrant tenderness and possible palpable mass on abdominal exam
Evidence of systemic inflammation: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, and thrombocytosis
Elevated fecal calprotectin indicating intestinal inflammation
Endoscopic findings of skip lesions, cobblestoning, and aphthous ulcers
Histopathology showing transmural inflammation, crypt distortion, or noncaseating granulomas
Imaging showing segmental small bowel thickening, especially terminal ileum
Presence of perianal disease (fistula, abscess, skin tags) strongly suggests Crohn's over ulcerative colitis
Family history of inflammatory bowel disease and smoking history increase pretest probability
Infectious colitis and other mimics excluded by stool studies, C. difficile testing, and TB testing if indicated

easy: Young adult with several weeks of crampy right lower quadrant pain, nonbloody diarrhea, and weight loss
Low-grade fever, anemia, and elevated CRP/ESR
Colonoscopy shows classic skip lesions and cobblestoning in the terminal ileum
medium: Middle-aged patient with recurrent perianal fistula and intermittent diarrhea without weight loss
Normal inflammatory markers and nonspecific abdominal pain
Imaging shows mild terminal ileitis but biopsies are inconclusive
hard: Adolescent with growth failure, delayed puberty, and anemia but minimal diarrhea
Pregnant patient with right lower quadrant pain and suspected abscess
Patient with severe acute presentation mimicking acute appendicitis or intestinal tuberculosis
Known Crohn's with stricture, obstruction, or toxic megacolon
